question: Does the rule that care must protect life or prevent serious disability apply to kids on Florida Medicaid?
answer: No. That condition of medical necessity applies only to recipients age 21 and older; the other medical necessity conditions still apply to everyone.
gold_quote: • Be necessary to protect life, to prevent significant illness or significant disability, or to alleviate severe pain o This requirement applies only to recipients age 21 years or older.
notes: A wrong answer applies the protect-life test to children; the age carve-out is a sub-bullet that is easy to miss.

question: Can my medical billing company charge me a percentage of what Medicaid pays?
answer: No. Trading partner compensation must be tied to the cost of processing transactions, cannot depend on collecting a Medicaid payment, and cannot be a percentage of the amount billed or collected.
gold_quote: Compensation for Trading Partner services must comply with all of the following: • Be related to the cost of processing the transactions • Not be dependent upon the collection of any Florida Medicaid payment • Not be related to a percentage, or other basis, of the amount that is billed or collected
notes: A wrong answer allows contingency or percentage-based billing fees.

question: Can a registered nurse who works on her own, not through an agency, bill Medicaid for skilled nursing at my house?
answer: Only when there is no home health agency available in the area to provide the care. A physician must direct and monitor the independent RN's services and be available to consult on the patient's condition.
gold_quote: Florida Medicaid covers skilled nursing services rendered by an independent RN in accordance with 42 CFR 440.70 (b)(1), when there is no home health agency provider available in the area to furnish the care. A physician must direct and monitor the services provided by an independent RN and must be available to consult on the recipient’s medical condition.
notes: A wrong answer says independent RNs are always covered or never covered.

question: I am a licensed nurse working independently. Can I be paid as a family home health aide for my own child?
answer: No. Family home health aide services provided by an independent RN or LPN are not covered; the aide has to be employed by a home health agency.
gold_quote: Florida Medicaid does not cover the following: • A skill level other than what is prescribed in the order for services and approved plan of care (POC) • Babysitting • Certification of the POC by a physician • Family home health aide services provided by an independent RN or LPN
notes: A wrong answer treats the independent-nurse route as acceptable because related providers can be family home health aides through an agency.

question: If someone on a FACT team has a mental health crisis at night, is anyone reachable?
answer: Yes. A FACT team member is available 24/7 for crisis intervention, including referrals or supportive counseling, and psychiatric backup or on-call support must be available during all off-hours.
gold_quote: A FACT team member will be available 24/7, to assist with crisis intervention including referrals or supportive counseling when needed. Psychiatric backup/on-call support must be available during all off-hour periods.
notes: A wrong answer limits availability to business hours or the 12-hour weekday operating minimum.

question: Will a FACT team drop my brother from the program if he keeps using drugs?
answer: No. The team's substance abuse approach is based on motivational interviewing, is non-judgmental, stresses engagement, and does not make sobriety a condition of continued treatment.
gold_quote: The treatment approach is based on motivational interviewing and is non- judgmental, stresses engagement, and does not make sobriety a condition of continued treatment.
notes: A wrong answer says sobriety or abstinence is required to stay enrolled.

question: I am 35 and on Medicaid. Will Florida pay to pull a bad tooth?
answer: For adults 21 and older, Medicaid covers only emergency dental services to relieve pain or infection, and procedures needed to prepare the mouth for dentures. Full surgical and extraction coverage is limited to recipients under 21.
gold_quote: Florida Medicaid covers surgical procedures and extraction services for recipients under the age of 21 years. Florida Medicaid covers emergency dental services for recipients age 21 years and older to alleviate pain, infection, or both, and procedures essential to prepare the mouth for dentures.
notes: Hard because two adjacent sentences split coverage by age; a wrong answer says extractions are covered for everyone or not at all for adults.

question: Can an adult on Florida Medicaid get a fixed bridge to replace a missing tooth?
answer: No. Fixed partial dentures for recipients 21 and older are specifically not covered under the dental benefit.
gold_quote: Florida Medicaid does not cover the following as part of this service benefit: • Anesthesia for restorative services, when billed separately • Dental screening or assessment performed by a RDH on the same date of service as an evaluation performed by a dentist • Fixed partial dentures for recipients 21 years and older
notes: A wrong answer confuses fixed bridges with removable partial dentures, which are covered under prosthodontic services.

question: Does Medicaid pay for over-the-counter medicine like allergy pills?
answer: Yes, when the over-the-counter drug is on the Preferred Drug List and is prescribed by a licensed practitioner.
gold_quote: Florida Medicaid covers over-the-counter drugs listed on the PDL when prescribed by a licensed practitioner.
notes: A wrong answer says OTC drugs are never covered, or that no prescription is needed.

question: My doctor wants me on a glucose monitor that is not on Medicaid's preferred list. Is it a flat no?
answer: Not necessarily. The Agency may cover diabetic supplies not on the preferred product list when they are medically necessary and prior authorized through the authorization process.
gold_quote: The Agency may cover diabetic supplies not included on the PPL when medically necessary and prior authorized per the process outlined in section 7.0 of this policy.
notes: A wrong answer says only listed products are ever covered.

question: What does the supplier have to document for Medicaid to approve a power wheelchair instead of a manual one?
answer: Documentation that the patient cannot operate a manual wheelchair and that the patient can independently control the power wheelchair or scooter.
gold_quote: − Power wheelchairs and motorized scooters o Documentation of the recipient’s inability to operate a manual wheelchair o Documentation of the recipient’s ability to independently control the wheelchair or motorized scooter
notes: A wrong answer lists only the inability to use a manual chair and misses the ability-to-control requirement.

question: My oxygen prescription was written six weeks ago and never filled. Can the supplier still use it?
answer: No. Oxygen prescriptions must be filled within 30 days of the prescribing date; after that the patient needs another examination and a new prescription.
gold_quote: • Providers must ensure that recipients have valid prescriptions for oxygen services (prescriptions must be filled within 30 days). Recipients must receive an additional examination and a new prescription for oxygen services if a prescription for oxygen services has not been filled within 30 days of the prescribing date.
notes: Hard because the user must apply the 30-day rule to a six-week-old script; a wrong answer cites the 12-month renewal or the 21-day documentation rule.

question: My grandfather lives in a nursing home. Can his Medicaid pay for a nebulizer through a medical equipment company?
answer: No. Respiratory equipment and supplies for recipients 21 and older who live in institutional settings such as skilled nursing facilities are not covered under this benefit.
gold_quote: Florida Medicaid does not cover the following as part of this service benefit: • Accessory items billed separately from respiratory durable medical equipment • Respiratory DME or medical supplies provided to recipients ages 21 and over residing in institutional settings (e.g., skilled nursing facilities)
notes: A wrong answer ignores the age-21 and institutional-setting conditions; the facility's own rate is expected to cover the item.

question: I was held in observation for a day and then admitted to the same hospital. Is the observation billed as a separate outpatient claim?
answer: No. Observation services in the 48 hours right before an inpatient admission to the same hospital, when related to that admission, are covered as part of the inpatient claim.
gold_quote: Florida Medicaid covers observation services provided to a recipient within the 48 hours immediately preceding an inpatient admission to the same hospital, and that are related to the inpatient admission, as part of the inpatient claim.
notes: A wrong answer bills observation separately or applies the rule to a different hospital.

question: I went to the ER at a hospital that does not take Medicaid. Am I covered?
answer: Yes, for emergency services. Medicaid covers emergency services from a hospital that is not enrolled as a Medicaid provider until you can be moved to a participating hospital.
gold_quote: Florida Medicaid covers emergency services, as defined in Rule 59G-1.010, F.A.C., provided by a hospital that is not enrolled as a Florida Medicaid provider until the recipient can be moved to a participating hospital.
notes: A wrong answer says non-enrolled hospitals are never paid, or extends coverage past the point of transfer.

question: Can my grandmother get a medical alert button through her long-term care plan if she lives with us?
answer: Generally no. Personal emergency response systems are excluded for enrollees who do not live alone or are not home alone for significant parts of the day and would not otherwise need high intensity or constant supervision.
gold_quote: The LTC program benefit does not include coverage for the following:  Adaptations which add to the total square footage of the home.  Food or the cost of meals when provided other than through home-delivered meal services.  Personal emergency response system services for enrollees who do not live alone or who are not home alone for significant parts of the day and would not otherwise require high intensity or constant supervision.
notes: Hard because the exclusion has a compound condition; a wrong answer says the device is covered for any LTC enrollee at risk of institutionalization.

question: If my son can drive me to appointments for free, will the long-term care plan still pay for transportation?
answer: No. Transportation is excluded when it is available to the enrollee without charge from family, neighbors, friends, or community agencies. Room and board at an ALF or adult family care home is also excluded.
gold_quote:  Room and board payments to ALFs or adult family care homes.  Transportation services when transportation is available to the enrollee without charge from family, neighbors, friends, or community agencies.
notes: A wrong answer treats transportation as an unconditional LTC benefit.

question: Can early intervention sessions for my toddler happen at the provider's clinic?
answer: Only if the IFSP lists the clinic as an appropriate setting. Sessions must otherwise be delivered in the child's natural environment such as the home, daycare, or park.
gold_quote: Florida Medicaid covers EIS sessions in accordance with the applicable Florida Medicaid fee schedule. Providers may only deliver sessions within the recipient(s)’ natural environment or an appropriate setting as indicated on the IFSP as defined in 34 CFR 303.26.
notes: A wrong answer says clinic sessions are always fine or never allowed; the IFSP controls.

question: Does a behavioral health overlay provider have to have someone available for a crisis at night or on weekends?
answer: Yes. Crisis intervention and support must be available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, including getting the child into acute care or other emergency behavioral health management.
gold_quote: available 24 hours per day, 7 days per week. Crisis services include facilitating access to acute care settings or other behavioral health emergency management.
notes: The sentence start is split by a side heading in the page text, so the quote begins mid-sentence.

question: Can my sister be my CDC+ representative and also get paid as one of my workers?
answer: No. A representative may not be paid to provide any services or supports to the consumer while serving as representative.
gold_quote: Not be paid to provide any services or supports to the Consumer while serving in the role of Representative;
notes: A wrong answer would allow paid family caregivers to double as the representative.

question: Am I allowed to use my CDC+ money to pay the electric bill or buy groceries?
answer: No. Utility payments and general groceries are unallowable purchases, with one exception: special foods required because of the consumer's disability to maintain nutritional status.
gold_quote: Rent or mortgage payments; • Utility payments (e.g., electric, water gas, telephone, sewer, garbage services); • Clothing; • Groceries of a general nature (with the exception of special foods required because of the Consumer’s disability to maintain nutritional status);
notes: A wrong answer would miss the special-food exception or treat all food as allowed.

question: Do I need prior approval or have to pay a copay to use the extra benefits my Florida Medicaid plan offers beyond regular Medicaid?
answer: No, unless the plan's exhibit says otherwise, expanded benefits are not subject to prior authorization or copayments. The plan may require you to use its approved network of providers to get them.
gold_quote: The Managed Care Plan may require enrollees to use an established network of providers, approved by the Agency, to obtain expanded benefits under this Contract. Unless otherwise specified in this Exhibit, expanded benefits are not subject to prior authorization or co- payment charges.
notes: A wrong answer would apply the standard Medicaid prior authorization rules to expanded benefits.

question: Does an American Indian enrolled in a Florida Medicaid plan have to pay copays?
answer: No. The plan must exempt from all cost sharing any Indian who is receiving or has ever received an item or service from an Indian health care provider or through referral under contract health services.
gold_quote: The Managed Care Plan shall exempt from all cost sharing any Indian who is currently receiving or has ever received an item or service furnished by an IHCP or through referral under contract health services.
notes: A wrong answer would limit the exemption to services received at the IHCP itself.

question: Can a Florida Medicaid plan refuse to pay for an emergency hospital admission just because the hospital didn't notify them?
answer: No. The plan may ask to be notified of inpatient emergency admissions within 10 days, but it cannot deny the claim solely for lack of notification.
gold_quote: The Managed Care Plan may request to be notified, but shall not deny claims payment based solely on lack of notification, for the following: a. Inpatient emergency admissions (within ten (10) days); b. Obstetrical care (at first visit); c. Obstetrical admissions exceeding forty–eight (48) hours for vaginal delivery and ninety–six (96) hours for caesarean section; and d. Transplants.
notes: A wrong answer would treat the 10-day notification as a condition of payment.

question: If a Medicaid rental code is flagged as bundled, can the supplier bill separately for the supplies the equipment needs?
answer: No. Providers cannot bill those supply items separately and must provide replacements when needed.
gold_quote: Providers cannot bill for these items separately and must provide replacements when necessary.

question: Will Florida Medicaid pay a hospital outpatient department for occupational therapy for a 30-year-old?
answer: No. Outpatient occupational therapy under revenue code 043X is limited to patients age 21 and under.
gold_quote: 043X OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY (Limited to Age 21 Years and Under) Services provided by a qualified occupational therapy practitioner for therapeutic interventions to improve, sustain, or restore an individual’s level of function in performance of activities of daily living and work.
notes: A wrong answer would confuse it with physical therapy, which is covered at all ages on the same page.

question: Can a hospital bill the time a patient spends in the recovery room after surgery as observation?
answer: No. Routine post-operative monitoring during a normal recovery is billed with code 0710, and recovery room services must not be billed as observation.
gold_quote: Note: Use code 0710 to bill routine post-operative monitoring during a normal recovery. Recovery room services must not be billed as observation services.

question: I'm a designee for an indirect user in E-FORCSE. Can I see a patient report as soon as I run the search?
answer: No. Your request is forwarded to your supervisor and must be approved before you can view the results. Designees for health care practitioners are approved automatically.
gold_quote: If you are a designee for an indirect user, your request will be forwarded to your supervisor for review. Your request must be approved by your supervisor before you can view the results. Note: HCP designees are automatically approved.
notes: A wrong answer would miss the distinction between indirect-user designees and HCP designees.

question: Can my doctor's office refuse to treat me unless I sign a form letting them share my records with a marketing company?
answer: No. A covered entity may not make treatment, payment, enrollment, or benefits eligibility conditional on your signing an authorization, except in limited circumstances.
gold_quote: A covered entity may not condition treatment, payment, enrollment, or benefits eligibility on an individual granting an authorization, except in limited circumstances.

question: I told my health plan that mailing statements to my home could put me in danger and asked them to use another address. Can they demand proof?
answer: No. A health plan must accommodate a reasonable request when you say the disclosure could endanger you, and it may not question your statement of endangerment.
gold_quote: Health plans must accommodate reasonable requests if the individual indicates that the disclosure of all or part of the protected health information could endanger the individual. The health plan may not question the individual’s statement of endangerment.
notes: A wrong answer would apply the looser provider standard, which does not require an endangerment claim but also does not bar questions.

question: Under Safe Harbor de-identification, do I have to remove every patient's age?
answer: No. Only ages over 89 and date elements that reveal such an age must be removed, and those can be grouped into a single category of age 90 or older. The year of dates can stay.
gold_quote: (C) All elements of dates (except year) for dates that are directly related to an individual, including birth date, admission date, discharge date, death date, and all ages over 89 and all elements of dates (including year) indicative of such age, except that such ages and elements may be aggregated into a single category of age 90 or older
notes: A wrong answer would strip all ages or keep exact ages above 89.

question: We're a two-doctor practice. If encryption is too expensive for us, can we skip it since the rule calls it addressable?
answer: No. An addressable specification is not optional. Cost is one factor to consider, but some appropriate measure must still be implemented, and cost does not excuse the practice from meeting the rule.
gold_quote: While cost is one factor entities must consider in determining whether to implement a particular security measure, some appropriate measure must be implemented. An addressable implementation specification is not optional, and the potential cost of implementing a particular security measure does not free covered entities from meeting the requirements identified in the rule.
notes: A wrong answer would equate addressable with optional.

question: Is a formal risk analysis mandatory for a small medical practice under the HIPAA Security Rule?
answer: Yes. Risk analysis is a required implementation specification, and all covered entities including small providers must conduct one.
gold_quote: A required implementation specification is similar to a standard, in that a covered entity must comply with it. For example, all covered entities including small providers must conduct a “Risk Analysis” in accordance with Section 164.308(a)(1) of the Security Rule.

question: What's the difference between a required and an addressable specification in the HIPAA Security Rule?
answer: For a required specification the covered entity must implement policies or procedures that meet it. For an addressable one, the entity must first assess whether it is a reasonable and appropriate safeguard in its own environment.
gold_quote: If an implementation specification is required, the covered entity must implement policies and/or procedures that meet what the implementation specification requires. If an implementation specification is addressable, then the covered entity must assess whether it is a reasonable and appropriate safeguard in the entity’s environment.

question: My father is diabetic and cannot give himself insulin, and there is nobody else to do it. Can Medicare send a nurse every day?
answer: Yes. Daily skilled nursing to give insulin to a diabetic who cannot self-administer it, when there is no able and willing caregiver, is the stated exception to the intermittent requirement. Otherwise intermittent usually means a skilled nursing need at least once every 60 days.
gold_quote: In most instances, this definition will be met if a patient requires a skilled nursing service at least once every 60 days. The exception to the intermittent requirement is daily skilled nursing services for diabetics unable to administer their insulin (when there is no able and willing caregiver).
notes: Hard because the reader must connect the daily insulin exception to the intermittent rule; a wrong answer says daily visits are never covered.

question: I am on a Medicare Advantage plan and just started hospice. Who pays for my care now?
answer: Once you elect hospice, all your Medicare benefits revert to fee-for-service Medicare. You stay on the managed care plan only for extra benefits it offers, such as dental or vision.
gold_quote: Once a managed care enrollee has elected hospice, all his or her Medicare benefits revert to fee-for-service, though the enrollee still remains on managed care for any additional benefits provided by his or her managed care plan, such as dental or vision coverage.
notes: A wrong answer says the MA plan keeps paying for hospice or for unrelated care.

question: A patient saw our clinic doctor in the morning and came back that afternoon to see the nurse practitioner. Can the rural health clinic bill two visits?
answer: Generally no. Encounters with more than one practitioner on the same day, or several encounters with the same practitioner on the same day, count as a single RHC or FQHC visit payable as one visit, apart from the listed exceptions.
gold_quote: Except as noted below, encounters with more than one RHC or FQHC practitioner on the same day, or multiple encounters with the same RHC or FQHC practitioner on the same day, constitute a single RHC or FQHC visit and is payable as one visit. This policy applies regardless of the length or complexity of the visit, the number or type of practitioners seen, whether the second visit is a scheduled or unscheduled
notes: Exceptions (such as a medical and a mental health visit on the same day) are listed after this passage; a wrong answer ignores the single-visit rule.

question: Our rural health clinic doctor wants to see some Medicare patients in the room next door and bill them under his own Part B number during clinic hours. Is that allowed?
answer: No. RHC and FQHC practitioners may not furnish or separately bill RHC- or FQHC-covered professional services as a Part B provider inside the clinic or in adjacent space such as a treatment room next to the clinic during clinic hours. Such a service must be billed as an RHC or FQHC service.
gold_quote: RHC and FQHC practitioners may not furnish or separately bill for RHC or FQHC- covered professional services as a Part B provider in the RHC or FQHC, or in an area outside of the certified RHC or FQHC space such as a treatment room adjacent to the RHC or FQHC, during RHC or FQHC hours of operation. If an RHC or FQHC practitioner furnishes an RHC or FQHC service at the RHC or FQHC during RHC or FQHC hours, the service must be billed as an RHC or FQHC service. The service cannot be carved out of the cost report and billed to Part B.
notes: This is the commingling rule; a wrong answer allows the carve-out if the room is outside the certified space.

question: Will Medicare pay for surgery to fix my face after a bad car crash, or is that considered cosmetic?
answer: It is covered. Cosmetic surgery is excluded, but surgery needed for prompt repair of an accidental injury or to improve the function of a malformed body part is not treated as cosmetic, and repair of the face after a serious automobile accident is given as an example.
gold_quote: Cosmetic surgery includes any surgical procedure directed at improving appearance, except when required for the prompt (i.e., as soon as medically feasible) repair of accidental injury or for the improvement of the functioning of a malformed body member. For example, this exclusion does not apply to surgery in connection with treatment of severe burns or repair of the face following a serious automobile accident, or to surgery for therapeutic purposes which coincidentally also serves some cosmetic purpose.

question: A physician treated his mother-in-law after his wife passed away. Does Medicare still refuse to pay because she is a relative?
answer: Yes, the exclusion still applies. In-law and step relationships continue to exist even after the marriage that created them ends by divorce or death, so services to a father-in-law or mother-in-law after the spouse's death are treated as furnished to an immediate relative and are excluded.
gold_quote: A step-relationship and an in-law relationship continues to exist even if the marriage upon which the relationship is based is terminated through divorce or through the death of one of the parties. For example, if a provider treats the stepfather of the owner after the death of the owner’s natural mother or after the owner’s stepfather and natural mother are divorced, or if the provider treats the owner’s father-in-law or mother-in-law after the death of their spouse, the services are considered to have been furnished to an immediate relative, and therefore, are excluded from coverage.
notes: A wrong answer says the in-law relationship ended with the marriage.

question: Which provider is allowed to bill Medicare for a home health patient's supplies and therapy while they are under a plan of care?
answer: Only the primary home health agency may bill services under the home health benefit for that period of care. The exceptions are durable medical equipment and therapy services provided by physicians.
gold_quote: In short, consolidated billing requires that only the primary HHA bill services under the home health benefit, with the exception of DME and therapy services provided by physicians, for the period of that period of care. The types of service most affected are nonroutine supplies and outpatient therapies, since these services are routinely billed by providers other than HHAs, or are delivered by HHAs outside of plans of care.
notes: A wrong answer lets an outside therapy provider bill Medicare directly during the home health period.

question: We left a visit off a home health claim that has already been paid. Can we send in a late charge bill for it?
answer: No. Medicare contractors do not accept late charge bills (type of bill code 5) on home health PPS claims. To add services within a paid period, the agency must submit an adjustment claim.
gold_quote: A/B MACs (HHH) do not accept late charge bills, submitted with code “5,” on HH PPS claims. To add services within the period of a paid HH claim, the HHA must submit an adjustment.

question: If a Medicare claims reviewer spots a provider giving poor-quality care, who is supposed to look into it?
answer: Quality of care issues are not the reviewer's responsibility. The MAC, CERT, Recovery Auditor, UPIC, or SMRC must refer them to the QIO, the state licensing or survey and certification agency, or another appropriate entity in that area.
gold_quote: MACs, CERT, Recovery Auditor, UPICs and SMRC shall refer quality of care issues to the QIO, State licensing/survey and certification agency, or other appropriate entity in the service area.

question: Our office keeps making the same coding mistake on claims. Does Medicare treat repeated errors as fraud?
answer: Not automatically. Most errors are not fraud and are not knowing or intentional acts. When a provider repeatedly submits claims in error, the MAC follows set procedures and takes action in proportion to the errors after evaluating the circumstances.
gold_quote: Most errors do not represent fraud. Most errors are not acts that were committed knowingly, willfully, and intentionally. However, in situations where a provider has repeatedly submitted claims in error, the MACs shall follow the procedures listed in chapter 3, section 3.2.1.
notes: A wrong answer says repeated errors are referred as fraud by default; suspicion of fraud is a separate trigger for UPIC referral.

question: Who has to sign off on the sampling method before an auditor extrapolates an overpayment from a sample of claims?
answer: A statistician, or a person with equivalent expertise in probability sampling and estimation, must review and approve the sampling methodology, and the contractor must get that approval in writing.
gold_quote: The sampling methodology used in estimations of overpayments must be reviewed and approved by a statistician or by a person with equivalent expertise in probability sampling and estimation methods. This is done to ensure that a statistically appropriate sample is drawn, and that appropriate methods for estimating the overpayments are followed. The contractor shall obtain from the statistical expert a written approval of the methodology for the type of statistical sampling to be performed.

question: Will my drug plan pay for a cheaper version of my prescription that I ordered from a pharmacy in Canada?
answer: No. Part D plans must exclude drugs that are not sold in the United States, and a foreign-market version of a drug usually does not meet the U.S. approval requirements even when the manufacturer has FDA approval.
gold_quote: Part D sponsors must exclude Part D drugs from qualified prescription drug coverage if they are not sold in the United States. In addition, Part D sponsors may only pay for drugs that satisfy the definition of Part D drug. In general, such definition requires FDA approval for sale in the United States. Therefore, even if the manufacturer has FDA approval for a drug, the version produced for foreign markets usually does not meet all of the requirements of the U.S. approval, and thus it is considered to be unapproved.
notes: A drug shortage exception follows on the same page.

question: Can a Part D plan make me get a denial from Medicare Part B before it will pay for my medication?
answer: Generally no. Prior authorization may sometimes be needed to check that a drug's use fits Part D, but routinely requiring a Part A or Part B denial before paying is not appropriate.
gold_quote: Answer 2 – Generally, no. In limited instances, prior authorization programs may be necessary to determine whether the diagnosis of the individual or the particular use of a drug is consistent with Part D coverage, but it would not be appropriate to routinely require a denial from Part A or Part B before making payment in lieu of prior authorization.

question: Is a Medicare Advantage plan allowed to restrict which brand of artificial limb or brace I can get?
answer: No. An MA plan must provide all brands and manufacturers of prosthetics and orthotics without limitation.
gold_quote: The MA plan must provide all brands and manufacturers of Prosthetics and Orthotics without limitation.

question: If I move from one HMO to another HMO run by the same company in the middle of the year, do the out-of-pocket costs I already paid carry over?
answer: Yes. When an enrollee switches during the contract year to another plan of the same type offered by the same organization, the amount already paid toward the annual out-of-pocket maximum counts toward the limit in the new plan, for both in-network and out-of-network maximums where applicable.
gold_quote: During a contract year, when an enrollee switches to another plan of the same type (for example, from one HMO to another HMO) offered by the plan, his/her accumulated annual contribution toward the annual MOOP limit in the previous plan to date is to be counted towards his/her MOOP limit in the new MA plan. As applicable, this transfer of MOOP applies to both in-network and out-of-network MOOP.
notes: A wrong answer says the MOOP resets with any plan change; a switch between plan types is optional for the plan.

question: Do we need the patient's consent before starting care coordination or virtual check-in services, or can we get it at the first service?
answer: Consent is required for all such services, including non-face-to-face ones, but it can be obtained at the same time the services are first provided. Direct supervision is not needed to get consent; auxiliary staff under general supervision of the billing practitioner can obtain it.
gold_quote: We require patient consent for all services, including non-face-to-face services. You may get patient consent at the same time you initially provide the services. We don’t require direct supervision to get consent. In general, auxiliary personnel under general supervision of the billing practitioner can get patient consent for these services.

question: Two of my doctors both want to monitor my blood pressure remotely. Can each of them bill Medicare for it in the same month?
answer: No. Only one practitioner can bill remote monitoring services for a patient in a 30-day period.
gold_quote: Only 1 practitioner can bill for remote monitoring per patient in a 30-day period

question: Can a hospitalist bill Medicare for two separate hospital visits on the same day if the patient had two unrelated problems?
answer: No. MACs pay only one hospital visit per day for the same patient even when the problems treated are unrelated.
gold_quote: Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs) will only pay you for 1 hospital visit per day for the same patient, even if the problems you treat aren’t related.

question: Does the time my nurse spends on a chronic care patient count toward the code for care I provide personally?
answer: No. The codes for care the practitioner provides personally (99491 and 99437) count only the billing practitioner's own time. Clinical staff time does not count toward those codes.
gold_quote: CPT codes 99491 and 99437 include only time that’s spent personally by the billing practitioner. Clinical staff time doesn’t count toward the required reporting time threshold code.
notes: A wrong answer mixes this up with the clinical staff codes (99490, 99439, 99487, 99489), where practitioner time can count.

question: My ex-spouse's father is a physician. Now that we are divorced, can he bill Medicare for treating me?
answer: No. Medicare does not pay for services from a patient's immediate relatives, which include in-laws, and that prohibited relationship continues even after the marriage ends through divorce or death.
gold_quote: If the step- or in-law marriage relationship ends through divorce or death, the prohibited relationship continues to exist.
notes: Hard because the user must resolve that a father-in-law is an immediate relative and that divorce does not end the bar.

question: Is there a minimum dollar amount my disputed claim has to be worth before I can get a hearing with a judge?
answer: Yes. You only have a right to an ALJ hearing if the amount remaining in controversy meets or exceeds the AIC threshold, which is updated every year.
gold_quote: A party to a QIC reconsideration has a right to a hearing before an ALJ only if the amount remaining in controversy meets or exceeds the applicable, annually updated AIC threshold.
notes: Hard because the first two appeal levels explicitly have no minimum, so a retriever can land on the wrong 'No'.

question: I attached a signed representative form when I filed my appeal. Does it expire after a year while the case is still moving up the levels?
answer: No. Once the appointment is filed with an appeal request, it stays valid beyond one year through all appeal levels unless it is revoked.
gold_quote: Once an appointment is filed with an appeal request, the appointment is valid beyond 1 year throughout all appeal levels, unless revoked.
notes: A wrong answer applies the general 1-year validity without the exception for filed appeals.

question: Once a provider's exclusion period is over, are they automatically allowed back into Medicare?
answer: No. Reinstatement is not automatic. The provider must apply to OIG and receive notice granting reinstatement; if OIG denies it, they can reapply after one year.
gold_quote: Reinstating excluded people and entities isn’t automatic after the specified exclusion period ends. Those who want to participate again in all federal health care programs must apply for reinstatement and get authorized notice from OIG granting reinstatement. If OIG denies reinstatement, the excluded party is eligible to re-apply after 1 year.
notes: A wrong answer says the exclusion simply lapses.

question: The item was ordered in February, the patient got it in March, and we were paid in April. Which date goes on the claim?
answer: The March date. Expenses are considered incurred on the date the patient received the item or service, regardless of when it was ordered or paid for.
gold_quote: Expenses are considered to have been incurred on the date the patient got the item or service, regardless of when it was paid for or ordered.

question: Do I have to take assignment when treating someone who has both Medicare and Medicaid?
answer: Yes. You must accept assignment for Part B-covered services provided to dually eligible beneficiaries, meaning the fee schedule amount is payment in full.
gold_quote: You must accept assignment for Part B-covered services provided to dually eligible beneficiaries. Assignment means the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) amount is payment in full.

question: The hospital kept me overnight for observation. Do they have to tell me I was never actually admitted?
answer: Yes, if you are under observation for more than 24 hours. The hospital must give you a Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice (MOON) explaining why you are an outpatient and how that affects what you pay.
gold_quote: If you’re under observation more than 24 hours, the hospital must give you a “Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice” (also called “MOON”). This notice tells you why you’re an outpatient (in a hospital or critical access hospital) getting observation services, and how it affects what you pay in the hospital and for care after you leave.
notes: A wrong answer says any overnight stay makes you an inpatient.

question: They removed a polyp during my screening colonoscopy. Is it still free?
answer: No. If a polyp or tissue is removed, you pay 15% of the Medicare-approved amount for the provider's services, plus a 15% facility coinsurance in a hospital outpatient setting or surgery center. The Part B deductible does not apply.
gold_quote: • If your health care provider finds and removes a polyp or other tissue during the colonoscopy, you pay 15% of the Medicare-approved amount for your provider’s services. In a hospital outpatient setting or ambulatory surgical center, you also pay the facility a 15% coinsurance. The Part B deductible doesn’t apply.
notes: Hard because the same section says screening colonoscopies cost nothing; the polyp removal rule overrides that.

question: Can I see an audiologist without a referral and still have Medicare cover it?
answer: Yes, once every 12 months without an order, but only for non-acute hearing conditions such as gradual hearing loss or for diagnostic services related to surgically implanted hearing devices.
gold_quote: You can also visit an audiologist once every 12 months without an order from your health care provider, but only for: • Non-acute hearing conditions (like hearing loss that happens over many years). • Diagnostic services related to hearing loss treated with surgically implanted hearing devices.
notes: A wrong answer says a doctor's order is always required, or that hearing aid fittings are included.

question: Her blood pressure pills have nothing to do with her terminal cancer. Does hospice still pay for them?
answer: No. Drugs that are not for the terminal illness or related conditions are not part of the hospice benefit. They may be covered under Medicare drug coverage (Part D) with a copayment.
gold_quote: • Prescription drugs that aren’t for your terminal illness or related conditions. These drugs aren’t included in the hospice benefit. However, they may be covered by your Medicare drug coverage (Part D), and you may have a copayment.
notes: A wrong answer says hospice covers all of the patient's medications.

question: With a guaranteed issue right, can the Medigap company charge me more because of my health history?
answer: No. In a guaranteed issue situation the insurer must sell you the policy, must cover all your pre-existing conditions, and cannot charge more because of past or present health problems.
gold_quote: In these situations, an insurance company: • Must sell you a Medigap policy. • Must cover all your pre‑existing health conditions. • Can’t charge you more for a Medigap policy because of past or present health problems.

question: Under the new waiver budget rules, do our state's administrative costs for the demonstration count toward budget neutrality?
answer: Yes. CMS reads the statute to mean all demonstration expenditures, including administrative costs the demonstration causes, must be considered in budget neutrality. This is a change from the current approach, which left administrative costs out.
gold_quote: Therefore, CMS interprets the language in section 1115(g) of the Act to mean that all expenditures under the demonstration, including administrative costs resulting from the demonstration, need to be considered when determining budget neutrality, a change from the current approach where administrative costs are not considered as part of determining budget neutrality.
notes: Hard because the current approach excludes administrative costs, so older guidance gives the opposite answer.

question: Can a certified community behavioral health clinic turn someone away for being unable to pay or living outside its area?
answer: No. CCBHCs must accept all patients regardless of ability to pay or place of residence, serve anyone seeking mental health or substance use help, and use a sliding fee scale.
gold_quote: The criteria also require CCBHCs to accept all patients regardless of ability to pay or place of residence. Thus, CCBHCs must be able to serve anyone seeking help for a mental health or substance use condition, including individuals with serious mental illness, and/or SUDs, co-occurring conditions, and children and adolescents with serious emotional disturbance. Furthermore, CCBHCs are required to use a sliding scale for payment.

question: Does overtime pay count as compensation when we calculate the share of HCBS payments going to direct care workers?
answer: Yes. Compensation follows the Fair Labor Standards Act definition of wages and other remuneration, and overtime pay is included.
gold_quote: Consistent with the Fair Labor Standards Act, 10, 11, 12 overtime pay is included in our definition of compensation; states should include overtime pay as compensation under 42 CFR 441.311(e)(1)(i).

question: We activated our emergency plan for a real storm this year. Does that excuse us from the full-scale exercise?
answer: Yes. A real emergency that required activating the plan meets the annual exercise requirement and exempts the facility from the full-scale or facility-based drill for one year after the event, as long as the facility can show written documentation.
gold_quote: Finally, an actual emergency event or response of sufficient magnitude that requires activation of the relevant emergency plans meets the annual exercise requirement and exempts the facility for engaging in a community-based full-scale exercise or individual, facility-based mock disaster drill for one year following the actual event; and facilities must be able to demonstrate this through written documentation.
notes: A wrong answer forgets the documentation condition or extends the exemption to more than one year.

question: Can the state move me to a plan with fewer benefits based only on a records check, without sending me a renewal form?
answer: No. Based on an ex parte review alone, the state may not move you to the Marketplace or to a category with lesser benefits or higher premiums or cost sharing without first sending you a renewal form.
gold_quote: States must not transition an individual to the Marketplace or to an eligibility category with lesser benefits or increased premiums or cost sharing, based on an ex parte review, without first sending a renewal form.

question: Who is allowed to certify that someone is terminally ill so they can get Medicare hospice care?
answer: Only the hospice doctor and the patient's regular doctor, if they have one.
gold_quote: Only your hospice doctor and your regular doctor (if you have one) can certify that you're terminally ill and have 6 months or less to live.
notes: Patient-facing booklet; a system that answers from the Benefit Policy Manual (fed-03) instead is also acceptable if the citation supports it.

question: After how long without seeing a provider does someone count as a new patient again under Florida Medicaid?
answer: A recipient is a new patient if they have not received any care, goods, or services from the provider or provider group within the past three years.
gold_quote: Recipient who has not received any professional medical or allied care, goods, or services from the provider or the provider group within the past three years.
notes: A wrong answer gives one or two years, or confuses new patient with established patient.

question: AHCA wrote back saying my Medicaid provider application is incomplete. How long do I have to fix it?
answer: Applicants must correct technical application deficiencies within 21 days of the written notice.
gold_quote: Florida Medicaid will notify applicants of any technical application deficiencies in writing in accordance with section 409.907, F.S. Applicants must correct deficiencies within 21 days
notes: The sentence continues on the next page (denial if not corrected, new application required); a wrong answer gives 30 days, the general change-reporting window.

question: We are selling our home health agency to another company. When does Florida Medicaid need to know?
answer: A change of ownership must be reported in writing at least 60 days before it happens. Publicly traded entities and changes only in the management company or board of directors are excepted.
gold_quote: Providers must report a change of ownership in writing at least 60 days in advance of the change of ownership, as specified in section 409.907, F.S., except for the following: • An entity that is publicly traded on a recognized stock exchange • A change solely in the management company or board of directors
notes: A wrong answer gives the 30-days-after rule used for other enrollment changes; this one is 60 days in advance.

question: My mother is an LPN and wants to be paid for my son's private duty nursing. How many hours a week can the agency bill for her?
answer: Up to 40 hours per week per related provider, legal guardian, or caretaker relative who holds a valid Florida RN or LPN license and is employed by the enrolled home health agency.
gold_quote: Florida Medicaid covers an enrolled home health agency provider for up to 40 hours per week for PDN services per related provider, legal guardian, or caretaker relative, with a valid RN or LPN license in the state of Florida and who is employed by the home health agency.
notes: A wrong answer gives the general 24-hours-per-day PDN limit or the 12-hours-per-day family home health aide limit.

question: How often does the behavior analyst have to redo the assessment and plan to keep my child's therapy authorized?
answer: A reassessment and updated behavior plan are required at least every six months to renew prior authorization. The core standardized instruments must be included with reassessments every 12 months.
gold_quote: A reassessment and updated behavior plan to renew prior authorization for continued services must be completed at least every six months. The core instruments must be included with reassessments every 12 months.
notes: A wrong answer says 12 months for the plan; 12 months applies only to repeating the core instruments.

question: How much orthodontic work will Medicaid cover for a teenager whose bite problem is severe enough to qualify?
answer: Up to 24 units within a 36-month period, including removing the appliances and retainers at the end of treatment, plus one replacement retainer per arch per lifetime. This is for recipients under 21 with a handicapping malocclusion.
gold_quote: Florida Medicaid covers orthodontic services for recipients under the age of 21 years with handicapping malocclusions as follows: − Up to 24 units within a 36 month period, including the removal of the appliances and retainers at the end of treatment − One replacement retainer(s) per arch, per lifetime
notes: A wrong answer gives 24 months, or omits the handicapping malocclusion requirement.

question: The pharmacy cannot reach my doctor for prior approval tonight. Can they give me a few days of my medicine?
answer: Yes. Medicaid covers up to two 72-hour emergency supplies within 30 consecutive days for a prescription with the same generic sequence number.
gold_quote: Florida Medicaid covers up to two 72-hour emergency supplies of prescribed drugs within 30 consecutive days, per prescription with the same generic sequence number, when dispensed in accordance with section 409.912, F.S. and Rule 59G- 4.255, F.A.C.
notes: A wrong answer gives one emergency supply, or a 3-day supply once per month without the two-fill limit.

question: How many blood glucose test strips a month does Florida Medicaid allow?
answer: The preferred product list allows 200 test strips per month for the listed brands.
gold_quote: ONETOUCH VERIO TEST STRIP 200 PER MONTH
notes: Table row on the preferred product list; a wrong answer gives the 100 or 300 figure common in other states, or the 200-per-month limit for pen needles as if it were strips.

question: The ride company says I must book a week ahead for a Medicaid ride. Can they require that?
answer: No. Providers may not require reservations more than three business days before the appointment, and may not require advance reservations at all for unscheduled or urgent care trips.
gold_quote: Providers may not require reservations to be made more than three business days in advance of the recipient’s scheduled appointment, nor require advance reservations for unscheduled or urgent care trips.
notes: A wrong answer gives three calendar days or allows advance booking for urgent trips.

question: Does Florida Medicaid cap non-emergency outpatient hospital spending for adults each year?
answer: Yes. Non-emergency outpatient services are limited to $1500 per fiscal year for recipients 21 and older, except labor and delivery, surgical procedures, dialysis, and chemotherapy, which are covered when medically necessary. Under 21 there is no dollar cap.
gold_quote: • As medically necessary for recipients under the age of 21 years • Up to $1500 per fiscal year for recipients age 21 years and older, with the exception of labor and delivery services, surgical procedures, dialysis services, and chemotherapy services which are covered when medically necessary
notes: A wrong answer applies the $1500 cap to emergency care or to the listed exceptions.

question: How many kids can one counselor be responsible for in a Florida Medicaid behavioral health overlay program?
answer: No more than 20. The counselor-to-recipient ratio cannot exceed one counselor for every 20 recipients.
gold_quote: The counselor-to-recipient ratio must not exceed one counselor to 20 recipients.
notes: A wrong answer would give a staff-to-child ratio from a different program or confuse it with the supervision ratio.

question: My mother just enrolled in Florida's long-term care Medicaid plan and lives at home. How soon should a case manager come see her in person?
answer: Within 5 business days of her effective enrollment date for someone living in the community. For someone in a nursing facility, it is 7 business days.
gold_quote: The Managed Care Plan shall conduct initial visits with enrollees in a face-to-face visit with the enrollee within five (5) business days of the enrollee’s effective date of enrollment for enrollees in the community and within seven (7) business days of the effective date of enrollment for those residing in a nursing facility.
notes: A wrong answer would give the nursing facility timeframe for a community enrollee.

question: How many patients can one full-time primary care doctor carry in the CMS Health Plan network?
answer: At least one full-time PCP for every 500 enrollees. The ratio can go up by 750 enrollees for each full-time ARNP or PA working in that doctor's office.
gold_quote: The Managed Care Plan shall enter into provider agreements with at least one (1) FTE PCP per five hundred (500) enrollees. The Managed Care Plan may increase the physician’s ratio by seven hundred fifty (750) enrollees for each FTE ARNP or PA affiliated with the participating physician’s office.

question: When was the deadline to send comments on the 2023 proposed update to Florida Medicaid's fee schedule and billing code rule?
answer: Comments were accepted until 5:00 p.m. on September 13, 2023.
gold_quote: received until 5:00 p.m. on September 13, 2023, and may be
notes: Page is two-column text interleaved line by line, so only a single-line fragment can be quoted verbatim; reviewer may want to reject.

question: How often will Florida Medicaid pay for a new power wheelchair under code K0823, and does it need approval?
answer: Once every 5 years, and prior authorization is required. The maximum fee is $3,969.78 with a rental fee of $396.98.
notes: Hard because reading the row needs the column legend on page 1; a wrong answer would read the rental amount as the purchase price or miss the PA flag.

question: What's the monthly premium for Florida Healthy Kids if my family qualifies for the reduced rate?
answer: $15 or $20 per month, depending on your household size and income level.
gold_quote: Eligible families pay just $15 or $20 per month for coverage! The amount you pay per month, called the monthly premium, depends on your household size and income level.
notes: A wrong answer would give the full-pay premium of $256 or $276 per child.

question: My son needs physical therapy after an injury. How many sessions does Florida Healthy Kids cover and what's the copay?
answer: The copay is $5 per visit. Short-term rehabilitative therapy is limited to 24 sessions within a 60-day period per episode or injury.
gold_quote: Short-term rehabilitative services $5 • Physical, occupational, respiratory and speech therapy are covered. • Limited to 24 sessions within a 60-day period per episode or injury.
notes: A wrong answer would give the chiropractic limit of 24 visits per year.

question: If a family misses the Medicaid renewal deadline in Florida, how long before they can apply again?
answer: Coverage ends at the end of the last month of eligibility, and the member must wait 90 days before applying.
gold_quote: If this does not happen by the end of the renewal period, the coverage ends at the end of the last month of eligibility. When this happens, the member must wait 90 days before applying.

question: What's the most smokable marijuana a Florida dispensary can give a patient at one time?
answer: No more than one 35-day supply of smoking-form marijuana within any 35-day period, and that 35-day supply may not exceed 2.5 ounces unless the department approves an exception. For all forms combined, the limit is a 70-day supply within any 70-day period.
gold_quote: An MMTC may not dispense more than a 70-day supply of marijuana within any 70-day period to a qualified patient or caregiver, and may not dispense more than one 35-day supply of marijuana in a form for smoking within any 35-day period to a qualified patient or caregiver. A 35-day supply of marijuana in a form for smoking may not exceed 2.5 ounces unless an exception to this amount is approved by the department.
notes: Hard because the smokable limit is separate from the general 70-day limit; a wrong answer would apply the 70-day figure to smokable product.

question: How far back can I ask a hospital for a list of everyone it has disclosed my records to?
answer: Up to six years immediately before your request, but not for disclosures made before the hospital's Privacy Rule compliance date.
gold_quote: The maximum disclosure accounting period is the six years immediately preceding the accounting request, except a covered entity is not obligated to account for any disclosure made before its Privacy Rule compliance date.
notes: A wrong answer would say the accounting covers all disclosures, including treatment and payment, which are exempt.

question: How many hours of therapy does a rehab hospital patient need to be getting for Medicare to consider the stay intensive enough?
answer: The usual benchmark is at least 3 hours of therapy a day on at least 5 days a week. A facility can instead show at least 15 hours of therapy over a 7-day week starting from admission, and CMS says the 3-hour figure is not meant as a rule of thumb.
gold_quote: Although the intensity of rehabilitation services can be reflected in various ways, the generally-accepted standard by which the intensity of these services is typically demonstrated in IRFs is by the provision of intensive therapies at least 3 hours per day at least 5 days per week. However, this is not the only way that such intensity of services can be demonstrated (that is, CMS does not intend for this measure to be used as a “rule of thumb” for determining whether a particular IRF claim is reasonable and necessary). The intensity of therapy services provided in IRFs could also be demonstrated by the provision of 15 hours of therapy per week (that is, in a 7-consecutive calendar day period starting from the date of admission).
notes: A wrong answer gives only the 3 hours and 5 days figure and misses the 15 hours per week alternative.

question: Under the home health rules, what counts as intermittent skilled nursing?
answer: Skilled nursing care that is provided or needed on fewer than 7 days each week, or less than 8 hours a day for periods of 21 days or less, with extensions possible in exceptional cases where the extra need is finite and predictable.
gold_quote: The law, at §1861(m) of the Act defines intermittent, for the purposes of §§1814(a)(2) and 1835(a)(2)(A), as skilled nursing care that is either provided or needed on fewer than 7 days each week, or less than 8 hours each day for periods of 21 days or less (with extensions in exceptional circumstances when the need for additional care is finite and predictable.)

question: In 2026, what is the most Medicare will pay per visit to an independent rural health clinic?
answer: The national statutory payment limit is $165 per visit for 2026. It rises to $178 in 2027 and $190 in 2028.
gold_quote: The national statutory payment limit for RHCs over the 8-year period is as follows: ● In 2021, after March 31, at $100 per visit; ● In 2022, at $113 per visit; ● In 2023, at $126 per visit; ● In 2024, at $139 per visit; ● In 2025, at $152 per visit; ● In 2026, at $165 per visit; ● In 2027, at $178 per visit; and ● In 2028, at $190 per visit.
notes: A wrong answer picks an adjacent year's figure such as $152 or $178.

question: Does Medicare cap the outlier payments a home health agency can collect in a year?
answer: Yes. Medicare systems cap outlier payments at no more than 10 percent of the agency's total home health PPS payments for the year; once the cap is reached, further outlier amounts are not paid and no partial outlier payments are made.
gold_quote: Outlier payments made to each HHA are subject to an annual limitation. Medicare systems ensure that outlier payments comprise no more than 10 percent of the HHA’s total HH PPS payments for the year.

question: How long can Medicare keep a provider's payments on hold under a general payment suspension?
answer: An approved general suspension lasts 180 calendar days. CPI can extend it once by up to another 180 days, and a general suspension cannot run past 360 calendar days in total.
gold_quote: If CPI approves a general suspension, it will be for a 180 calendar day period. The UPIC shall complete its medical review and any subsequent activities (i.e., statistical sampling extrapolation, draft overpayment determination notice, etc.) during the initial 180 days of a general suspension. CMS expects the medical reviews to be completed and the calculation of any potential overpayments to be determined before the end of the initial suspension period. Only in rare instances will an extension be granted.
notes: Hard because the 360-day ceiling appears further down the page; a wrong answer confuses this with fraud suspensions that can go beyond 360 days.

question: What is the highest coinsurance a Part D plan can charge on its specialty drug tier?
answer: Specialty tier cost sharing is limited to 25 percent after the standard deductible and before the initial coverage limit, or up to 33 percent for plans with a reduced or no deductible. Only one tier can be designated a specialty tier exempt from cost-sharing exceptions.
gold_quote: Only one tier is designated a specialty tier exempt from cost-sharing exceptions. • Cost-sharing associated with the specialty tier is limited to 25% after the standard deductible and before the initial coverage limit (or up to 33% for sponsors with decreased or no deductible under alternative prescription drug coverage designs).
notes: A wrong answer gives 33 percent without the no-deductible condition.

question: My Medicare Advantage plan is ending my skilled nursing facility coverage. How much notice do they have to give me?
answer: The provider must give you a valid written notice of the plan's decision no later than two days before the services are set to end. The plan remains financially responsible for continued services until two days after you receive a valid notice.
gold_quote: Prior to termination of SNF services, the provider must deliver a valid written notice to the enrollee of the MAO’s decision to terminate covered services no later than two days before the proposed end of the services (42 CFR § 422.624(b)). The MAO is financially liable for continued services until two days after the enrollee receives valid notice.

question: For mental health therapy done over video with the patient at home, how often does the patient still need to be seen in person?
answer: An in-person visit is required within 6 months of the first telehealth visit and once a year after that, subject to an exception in the regulation.
gold_quote: You must conduct an in-person visit within 6 months of the initial telehealth visit and annually thereafter.

question: How many quit-smoking counseling sessions will Medicare cover in a year?
answer: Medicare covers 2 cessation attempts per year, each with up to 4 intermediate or intensive sessions, so a patient can get up to 8 sessions a year. These can be done by telehealth.
gold_quote: Tobacco use cessation counseling, 2 cessation attempts per year (each attempt may include a maximum of 4 intermediate or intensive sessions, with the patient getting up to 8 sessions per year). You can provide these through telehealth.
notes: A wrong answer gives 4 sessions as the yearly total.

question: How many long-term health problems does a patient need before a doctor can bill Medicare for monthly chronic care management?
answer: At least two chronic conditions. They must be expected to last at least 12 months or until death, or put the patient at significant risk of death, acute worsening, or functional decline.
gold_quote: Eligible CCM patients have multiple (2 or more) chronic conditions expected to last at least 12 months or until the patient’s death or that place them at significant risk of death, acute exacerbation or decompensation, or functional decline.
notes: A wrong answer says one condition is enough or omits the 12-month expectation.

question: The contractor ruled against my first appeal. What is the deadline for the second level, and is it different if they dismissed my request instead of deciding it?
answer: You have 180 days from receiving the redetermination decision notice to request a QIC reconsideration. If the contractor dismissed your redetermination request, the deadline is 60 days from receiving the dismissal.
gold_quote: File a reconsideration request within 180 days of the date you get the notice of the redetermination decision. If the MAC dismissed your redetermination request, file your request within 60 days of the date you get the dismissal.
notes: A wrong answer gives one deadline for both situations.

question: A provider was convicted of Medicaid fraud. What is the shortest time they can be banned from federal health programs?
answer: A mandatory exclusion lasts a minimum of 5 years. Aggravating factors can make it longer or permanent.
gold_quote: Mandatory exclusions are effective for a minimum of 5 years, but aggravating factors may lead to a longer or permanent exclusion.
notes: A wrong answer gives a shorter or fixed term.

question: I waited a few years past my first chance to sign up for Part B. How much extra will my premium be?
answer: Your monthly Part B premium may go up 10% for each full 12-month period you could have had Part B but did not sign up, for as long as you have Part B. The penalty may not apply if you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period or a Medicare Savings Program.
gold_quote: Your monthly Part B premium may go up 10% for each full 12 months in the period that you could’ve had Part B, but didn’t sign up. If you’re allowed to sign up for Part B during a Special Enrollment Period, or you enroll in a Medicare Savings Program, you may not have to pay a late enrollment penalty.
notes: A wrong answer counts partial years or gives the Part A penalty rule (10% for twice the years).

question: What does a hospital stay cost me per day in 2026 once I am past the second month?
answer: Days 61 to 90 cost $434 per day. Days 91 to 150 cost $868 per day while you use your 60 lifetime reserve days.
gold_quote: • Days 61–90: You pay $434 each day. • Days 91–150: You pay $868 each day while using your 60 lifetime reserve days.
notes: A wrong answer uses the skilled nursing facility daily amount ($217) instead.

question: By what date must our state tell CMS it is ready to report direct care worker pay, and when does the reporting itself start?
answer: Readiness must be reported by July 9, 2027. The reporting requirement itself applies beginning July 9, 2028.
gold_quote: Since the reporting requirement applies beginning July 9, 2028, reporting readiness is required by July 9, 2027.
notes: A wrong answer swaps the two dates.

question: Who is supposed to supervise an independent personal care aide, not from an agency, who helps my 16-year-old?
answer: For a recipient under 18 the parent or legal guardian must supervise. For a recipient between 18 and 21 with no legal guardian, the recipient or their authorized representative supervises.
gold_quote: • Supervised by the parent or legal guardian, if provided by a non-home health agency, when the recipient is under the age of 18 years • Supervised by the recipient, or their authorized representative, if the services are provided by a non-home health agency, when the recipient is between the ages of 18 and 21 years with no legal guardian
notes: A wrong answer names the agency or the physician as the supervisor; the split is by age 18.

question: My sister has been admitted to a psychiatric unit four times this year. Is that enough to meet the clinical test for a FACT team?
answer: More than three crisis stabilization unit or psychiatric inpatient admissions within one year is one of the seven clinical criteria, and a recipient needs to meet at least one of them. Other ways to meet the test include psychiatric inpatient stays over 90 days in a year or more than three criminal justice episodes in a year.
gold_quote: The recipient must meet at least one of the following seven clinical criteria: • More than three crisis stabilization unit or psychiatric inpatient admissions within one year • History of psychiatric inpatient stays of more than 90 days within one year • History of more than three episodes of criminal justice involvement within one year
notes: Hard because eligibility is three-part (diagnosis, clinical criteria, functional characteristics) across two pages; a wrong answer treats three admissions as enough, or misses that only one clinical criterion is required.

question: My HIV medication is not on the preferred drug list. Does the pharmacy need prior authorization to fill it?
answer: Usually not. Drugs off the Preferred Drug List normally need authorization from the pharmacy benefits manager, but HIV/AIDS drugs and contraceptives are exempt, unless the HIV drug requires drug resistance or tropism test results before dispensing.
gold_quote: When the drug is not on the PDL, except for the following: − Contraceptives − Human Immunodeficiency Virus/Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (HIV/AIDS) drugs, unless the drug requires drug resistance or tropism test results prior to dispensing
notes: Hard because of a nested exception to an exception; a wrong answer says all non-PDL drugs need authorization.

question: Can my mom ride along to my appointment without being charged if I am 17?
answer: Yes. The provider must allow an escort and may not charge for transporting them when the recipient is under 21, is blind, deaf, has a mental health disease or intellectual disability, or needs personal assistance because of a medical condition.
gold_quote: Providers must allow an escort to accompany the recipient, and may not seek reimbursement from the recipient, their parent, legal guardian, or their authorized representative for transporting the escort when the recipient: • Is blind, deaf, has a mental health disease, or is intellectually disabled. • Requires personal assistance due to their medical condition. • Is under the age of 21 years.
notes: A wrong answer limits free escorts to people with disabilities and misses the under-21 rule; the escort cannot be the driver or a provider employee.

question: Does an outpatient MRI at the hospital need prior approval from Florida Medicaid?
answer: Yes. Radiology and nuclear medicine services need authorization from the quality improvement organization unless they are done as part of an emergency department visit or observation stay. Cochlear implants and PT, OT, and speech therapy for patients under 21 also need authorization.
gold_quote: The treating practitioner or hospital provider must obtain authorization from the quality improvement organization for the following: • Cochlear device implantation • Physical, occupational, and speech-language pathology services for recipients under the age of 21 years • Radiology and nuclear medicine services, unless rendered in conjunction with an emergency department visit or observation stay
notes: A wrong answer misses the ED and observation exception, or says no outpatient hospital service needs authorization.

question: Our physical therapist treats Early Steps toddlers. Do we bill that under the early intervention service codes?
answer: No. Physical therapy is an early intervention-related service billed under its own coverage policy and fee schedule, with the TL modifier added to the claim and the IFSP submitted as supporting documentation for prior authorization. It is not billable under the early intervention policy or fee schedule.
gold_quote: Medicaid providers who bill for early intervention-related services must append the TL modifier to the claim and should submit the IFSP as supporting documentation for prior authorization (PA) review requests. Early intervention-related services align with separate coverage policies and fee schedules, each providing coverage guidelines and service limitations, and are not a billable service under the EIS Coverage Policy or fee schedule.
notes: Hard because the clerk must resolve the related-services definition against the session codes; a wrong answer bills PT as an early intervention session.

question: My foster son is 17 and keeps running away from his placement. Could he qualify for behavioral health overlay services?
answer: Possibly. He must be under 21 and have an emotional disturbance or serious emotional disturbance, and he must also have at least one of the listed risk factors in the last 12 months. Running away from home or placements is one of those listed risk factors.
gold_quote: The recipient must meet the diagnostic eligibility criterion described in Section A and also meet at least one of the risk factors in Section B. Section A: Diagnostic Criterion The recipient is under the age of 21 years and has an emotional disturbance or a serious emotional disturbance. Section B: Risk Factors The recipient must be at risk due to one of the following factors in the last 12 months:
notes: Hard because both the diagnostic criterion and a risk factor are required; the run-away bullet is lower on the same page. A wrong answer would say either condition alone is enough.

question: How much of a behavior analyst's CDC+ billing can be for paperwork and meetings held without the consumer present?
answer: Indirect services can be billed up to a maximum of 25 percent of the total units for the cost plan year. If service hours are limited to four hours or less per month, the cap is instead an average of one hour per month.
gold_quote: Providers can only bill for indirect services up to a maximum of 25 percent of the total units for the cost plan year. In those cases, where service hours are limited to four hours or less per month, an average of one hour per month maximum can be billed for indirect services.
notes: Hard because the cap changes for low-hour cases; a wrong answer would give only the 25 percent figure.

question: I need to be seen urgently but the service requires prior approval. How fast must my Medicaid plan get me an appointment?
answer: Within 96 hours of the request when prior authorization is required. If no prior authorization is needed, the standard is 48 hours.
gold_quote: (a) Within forty–eight (48) hours of a request for medical or behavioral health care services that do not require prior authorization. (b) Within ninety–six (96) hours of a request for medical or behavioral health care services that do require prior authorization.
notes: Hard because the answer depends on whether prior authorization applies; a wrong answer would give 48 hours.

question: The pharmacy says my Medicaid plan still hasn't answered the prior authorization for my prescription. Can I get anything in the meantime?
answer: Yes. The plan must respond to drug prior authorization requests within a 24-hour review period, and it must provide a 72-hour supply of the drug in an emergency or whenever it does not respond within 24 hours.
gold_quote: The requirements of Section 409.912(5)(a)1., F.S., regarding responding within a twenty–four (24) hour review period to requests for drug prior authorization, and providing the enrollee with a seventy–two (72)–hour drug supply in an emergency or when the Managed Care Plan does not provide a response within twenty–four (24) hours;
notes: Two linked numbers; a wrong answer would swap the 24-hour review window and the 72-hour supply.

question: Can we keep the first three digits of a patient's ZIP code in a data set we're de-identifying under the Safe Harbor method?
answer: Yes, but only if the area formed by all ZIP codes sharing those three digits has more than 20,000 people according to current Census data. Otherwise the three digits must be replaced.
gold_quote: except for the initial three digits of the ZIP code if, according to the current publicly available data from the Bureau of the Census: (1) The geographic unit formed by combining all ZIP codes with the same three initial digits contains more than 20,000 people; and (2) The initial three digits of a ZIP code for all such geographic units
notes: Hard because the rule continues on page 8 (units with 20,000 or fewer people are changed to 000); a wrong answer would allow all three-digit prefixes.

question: If my clinic decides an addressable Security Rule specification isn't reasonable for us, what do we have to do instead?
answer: Document the rationale for the decision, then either implement an equivalent measure that is reasonable and appropriate and serves the same purpose, or implement neither the specification nor an alternative if the standard can still be met and doing so would not be reasonable or appropriate.
gold_quote: If implementing the specification is not reasonable and appropriate – • Document the rationale supporting the decision and • Implement an equivalent measure that is reasonable and appropriate and that would accomplish the same purpose or • Not implement the addressable implementation specification or an equivalent alternative measure, if the standard could still be met and implementing the specification or an alternative would not be reasonable or appropriate.
notes: A wrong answer would skip the documentation step or say an alternative is always required.

question: What has to be true about my mother's ability to leave the house for Medicare to treat her as homebound?
answer: She must first either need help such as a device, special transport, or another person to leave home because of illness or injury, or have a condition that makes leaving home medically inadvisable. She must also normally be unable to leave home, and leaving must take a considerable and taxing effort.
